title: Seva beyond the gurdwara
hookLine: service is for everyone, not only Sikhs
tomorrow: maya's grandma runs a food bank shelf. is that langar too?

lines: THEY DON'T GO TO THE GURDWARA.
cards: Simran is holding a foil tray of dal and rice from langar, still warm, for Kiran's family. Kiran's mom is home from the hospital and nobody has had time to cook. But at Kiran's front door, Simran hesitates.
They don't go to the gurdwara. Will this be weird? Will it look like she's trying to recruit them?
Then she remembers a strange story Bebe tells, about a man who gave water to the enemy.

teach.b: Here's the odd detail. Tradition says that during the fighting at Anandpur, a Sikh named Bhai Kanhaiya walked the battlefield with a water bag, giving water to the wounded. All of them.
Including the soldiers fighting against the Sikhs.
Some Sikhs were furious and brought him to Guru Gobind Singh. He's helping the enemy. And the puzzle is the Guru's answer.
Tradition says he didn't scold Bhai Kanhaiya. He gave him ointment too, and told him to dress their wounds as well. How does that make sense?
Bhai Kanhaiya's own answer, as the story tells it: he didn't see Sikhs or enemies.

teach.h: THE GURU'S FACE IN EVERY FACE.
teach.b: He saw the Guru's face in every face.
A line in the Akal Ustat, in the Dasam Granth, puts it plainly: recognize the whole human race as one. Manas ki jaat. One human race.
That's the line to tell a friend tonight.

So seva beyond the gurdwara isn't a way to win anyone over, and it isn't a favor kept for your own. It's the same water, for whoever is thirsty. Kiran's mom opens the foil, smells the dal, and says, oh.
Then she cries a little, and laughs at herself for crying.

how: Sikh seva, including langar and relief work, is offered to anyone regardless of religion or background; Bhai Kanhaiya's story is often told to explain why.

games.q: what does “seva beyond the gurdwara” mean?
o: service for anyone, beyond your own community
service done only on Sikh holy days
service that brings new members to the faith

games.q: beyond the walls — tap the pairs.
p: recognize the human race as one

s: seva is meant to help your own community first
Bhai Kanhaiya gave water to every wounded soldier, and the Guru added ointment.
tradition says Guru Gobind Singh gave Bhai Kanhaiya ointment for the wounded on both sides
instead of scolding him, he widened the seva.

games.q: you volunteer with a Sikh group serving free meals downtown. a friend asks: is it only for Sikhs, or a way to win people over? what's the honest answer?
o: neither: it's for whoever is hungry, because the human race is one.
mostly for Sikhs, but others are welcome if there's food left over.
partly to show people the faith, so some of them might join.
games.why: Bhai Kanhaiya gave water to every wounded soldier, and the Guru approved. seva beyond the walls doesn't sort people or recruit them.

practice: Count on your fingers people who have helped you who weren't from your own circle: a nurse, a neighbor, a stranger who held a door, a teacher from another background. Give each one a quiet thank-you.
Let the last finger rest, and sit.

wordCard.voice: Seva beyond the gurdwara. Service for anyone, of any background, asking nothing back. Manas ki jaat: the human race, one.

carryVoice: Beyond the walls: the same water, for whoever is thirsty, whoever they are. Take care.

sources.ref: Sikh tradition: Bhai Kanhaiya giving water to the wounded of both sides at Anandpur, and Guru Gobind Singh's response
Akal Ustat (Dasam Granth), the verse beginning 'manas ki jaat sabai ekai pahichanbo', paraphrased
